title: How do sealed classes help implement algebraic data types (ADTs)?
shortTitle: How do sealed classes help implement algebraic data types (ADTs)?

s1_definition.profdef: An algebraic data type is a type formed by combining other types, principally as a *sum type* (a value is exactly one of several named variants) and a *product type* (a value bundles several fields together). Sealed types give Java sum types: a sealed interface or class with a closed set of permitted subtypes models "one of these variants," and records model product types by bundling fields. Together, sealed types plus records plus exhaustive pattern-matching `switch` give Java a complete, type-safe encoding of ADTs, with the compiler enforcing that every variant is handled.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India describes a payment outcome as being exactly one of a fixed set of shapes: it is a Success carrying an amount, or a Failure carrying a reason, or a Pending carrying an expected date — never two at once, and never some unknown fourth shape. A sealed type is how the bank writes down that closed "it is exactly one of these" list (the sum), and a record is how each shape bundles its own data (the product). When a clerk processes an outcome, a checklist with one row per shape is guaranteed complete, so no outcome is ever mishandled. That closed "one of these bundles" model is an algebraic data type.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sealed types provide the closed sum ("one of these variants"), records provide the product (bundled fields), and exhaustive `switch` makes handling them type-safe and complete.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An algebraic data type is a type formed by combining other types, principally as a *sum type* (a value is exactly one of several named variants) and a *product type* (a value bundles several fields together). Sealed types give Java sum types: a sealed interface or class with a closed set of permitted subtypes models "one of these variants," and records model product types by bundling fields. Together, sealed types plus records plus exhaustive pattern-matching `switch` give Java a complete, type-safe encoding of ADTs, with the compiler enforcing that every variant is handled.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India describes a payment outcome as being exactly one of a fixed set of shapes: it is a Success carrying an amount, or a Failure carrying a reason, or a Pending carrying an expected date — never two at once, and never some unknown fourth shape. A sealed type is how the bank writes down that closed "it is exactly one of these" list (the sum), and a record is how each shape bundles its own data (the product). When a clerk processes an outcome, a checklist with one row per shape is guaranteed complete, so no outcome is ever mishandled. That closed "one of these bundles" model is an algebraic data type.

**One line to remember:** Sealed types provide the closed sum ("one of these variants"), records provide the product (bundled fields), and exhaustive `switch` makes handling them type-safe and complete.

sections.s2_technical:
An **algebraic data type** has two building blocks. A **product type** is a bundle of fields, like a pair or a struct — in Java a `record` is exactly this, combining several component values into one immutable type. A **sum type** (also called a tagged union or variant type) says a value is exactly one of several alternatives — this is what Java lacked a clean way to express until sealed types. Combining sums of products is what "algebraic" means: the set of possible values is built by adding up alternatives, each of which multiplies together its fields.

**Sealed types deliver the sum.** A `sealed interface Result permits Success, Failure, Pending` declares that a `Result` is exactly one of three variants, and the `permits` clause closes the set so no other variant can exist. Each variant is typically a **record** (the product part), bundling that variant's own fields, for example `record Success(BigDecimal amount)` and `record Failure(String reason)`. Because records are implicitly final, they satisfy the sealed-subtype rule automatically. This gives a precise, closed "sum of products" exactly like ADTs in functional languages such as Haskell or Scala.

The third ingredient is **exhaustive pattern matching**. A `switch` over the sealed type with a case per variant, using record patterns to destructure the fields, is checked by the compiler for completeness, so you cannot forget a variant and you do not need a `default`. This is the "safe consumption" side of ADTs: defining the data as a closed sum is only half the value; the other half is that every place that consumes it is forced to handle all cases. If you add a variant, every non-exhaustive switch fails to compile.

This pattern shines for modelling **domain states and results**. Instead of a single mutable class with nullable fields and a status enum — where illegal combinations like "status is SUCCESS but reason is set" are possible — an ADT makes **illegal states unrepresentable**: a `Success` simply has no `reason` field, and a `Failure` simply has no `amount` field. The type system prevents the invalid combinations that a flat class would allow. In banking this eliminates a whole category of bugs around half-populated objects.

A senior nuance is that ADTs encourage **total functions**: a function that maps every variant to a result, verified exhaustive by the compiler, which is far safer than scattered `instanceof` chains or status flags. Another nuance is that sealed-plus-records ADTs compose recursively, letting you model trees and expression grammars, such as a sealed `Expr permits Add, Mul, Literal`, which is the classic interpreter pattern done type-safely. A final nuance is that ADTs pair naturally with immutable records for thread-safe, value-based domain modelling, which suits a bank's need for auditable, side-effect-free representations of money states, and the exhaustiveness guarantee means regulatory changes that add a new state are caught at compile time everywhere they must be handled.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India represents the outcome of a payment as one of exactly three shapes: a success with a settled amount, a failure with a reason, or a pending with an expected date. In the past the bank used one class with a status enum and nullable amount and reason fields, which allowed invalid combinations and caused bugs. We model it as a sealed sum of record products so illegal states cannot be represented.

Problem 2 — Every consumer of a payment outcome must handle all three shapes. We use an exhaustive pattern switch with record destructuring so the compiler guarantees completeness, and adding a future shape would break the build at every unhandled site.

Problem 3 — The bank also models a small expression ADT for fee formulas — add, multiply, literal — to show the recursive, interpreter-style power of sealed-plus-records ADTs, evaluating a formula safely.

In the mini-project we define a sealed `PaymentOutcome` with record variants `Success`, `Failure`, and `Pending`, an exhaustive handler, and a recursive sealed `Expr` with `Literal`, `Add`, `Mul` plus an evaluator, logging results.

The code contains: the sum-of-products outcome type, an exhaustive consumer, a recursive expression ADT with an evaluator, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three payment outcomes — a success of 50,000, a failure for insufficient funds, a pending with an expected date — and a fee formula (1000 + 500) times 2.

Step 1 — The sealed `PaymentOutcome` declares that an outcome is exactly one of three record variants. Each record carries only its own fields, so a success has an amount but no reason, and a failure has a reason but no amount. This makes invalid combinations impossible to construct, unlike a flat class with nullable fields.

Step 2 — The handler's `message` method runs an exhaustive `switch` with record patterns. Because the type is sealed, the compiler verifies all three variants are covered and needs no `default`. Each case destructures the record directly into its fields.

Step 3 — The success case prints the reference and settled amount, the failure case prints the reference and reason, and the pending case prints the reference and expected date. Each outcome is handled totally and safely.

Step 4 — The recursive `Expr` ADT models a fee formula as a tree: a multiply of an add of two literals and another literal. The static `eval` method switches over the three expression variants, recursing into sub-expressions.

Step 5 — Evaluation computes 1000 plus 500 to get 1500, then multiplies by 2 to get 3000, using `BigDecimal`. The result is logged. This shows the interpreter pattern done with full compile-time exhaustiveness, impossible to get a missing-case bug.

```
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] SUCCESS TXF-1: settled Rs.50000
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] FAILURE TXF-2: Insufficient funds
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] PENDING TXF-3: expected 2026-10-28
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] Fee formula evaluates to Rs.3000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  SUM of PRODUCTS:
    sealed PaymentOutcome = Success(amount) | Failure(reason) | Pending(date)
       │ illegal states unrepresentable (no nullable mix)
       ▼
    message(o) → switch (exhaustive, record destructuring, no default):
       Success(ref, amount) → "SUCCESS ref settled Rs.amount"
       Failure(ref, reason) → "FAILURE ref reason"
       Pending(ref, date)   → "PENDING ref expected date"

  RECURSIVE ADT:
    Expr = Literal(v) | Add(l, r) | Mul(l, r)
       Mul( Add( Literal(1000), Literal(500) ), Literal(2) )
         eval → (1000 + 500) * 2
              →  1500 * 2
              →  3000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Algebraic data types are types built by combining other types, mainly as sum types and product types. A product type bundles several fields together, and a sum type says a value is exactly one of several named alternatives. Java gives me product types through records and sum types through sealed types, and together with exhaustive pattern matching they give me a complete, type-safe encoding of ADTs just like functional languages have.

Sealed types deliver the sum. A sealed interface with a permits clause declares that a value is exactly one of a closed set of variants, and each variant is typically a record that bundles its own fields, which is the product part. Because records are implicitly final they satisfy the sealed-subtype rule automatically, so I get a precise closed sum of products. In my banking project I model a payment outcome as a sealed type permitting success, failure, and pending, where success carries an amount, failure carries a reason, and pending carries an expected date.

The big win is that ADTs make illegal states unrepresentable. With the old approach of one class holding a status enum plus nullable amount and reason fields, I could accidentally have a success that also had a failure reason set, which is a bug waiting to happen. With the ADT, a success simply has no reason field and a failure has no amount field, so the invalid combinations cannot even be constructed. The type system prevents a whole category of half-populated-object bugs, which is exactly what a bank wants for money states.

The third ingredient is exhaustive pattern matching, which is the safe-consumption side. I consume the outcome with a switch that has a case per variant and destructures the record fields, and because the type is sealed the compiler verifies the switch is complete and needs no default. That makes my handlers total functions, and if a regulatory change adds a new outcome variant, every non-exhaustive switch fails to compile, pointing me to every place that must be updated. The same pattern composes recursively, so I also model a fee-formula expression as a sealed add, multiply, and literal and evaluate it with a total interpreter. So sealed types plus records plus exhaustive switch are how I implement algebraic data types in Java, giving me closed, immutable, compiler-checked domain models.
